entities.description: The Rider-Waite-Smith Tarot (1909), designed by Arthur Edward Waite and illustrated by Pamela Colman Smith, published by Rider & Company. The most widely used tarot deck in the English-speaking world. First deck to fully illustrate all 78 cards including the minor arcana pip cards.

The Thoth Tarot (1944), designed by Aleister Crowley and painted by Lady Frieda Harris. Based on projective geometry and Crowley's Thelemic philosophy. Published posthumously after Crowley's death in 1947.

The Tarot de Marseille, the dominant tarot pattern from the 17th century onwards. A standardised French/Italian tradition with pip-only minor arcana. Numerous variants exist; the Conver 1760 and Noblet 1650 are among the oldest surviving examples.

The 36-card Lenormand deck, named after the French cartomancer Marie Anne Lenormand (1772–1843), though the modern deck format was not designed by her. A distinct fortune-telling system using playing card imagery with symbolic overlays.
The standard 52-card French-suited playing card deck with two jokers (54 total). The ancestral form from which tarot decks derive, or a parallel development from the same Mamluk card tradition.

The Etteilla Tarot (1789) was the first tarot deck designed specifically for occult divination, created by Jean-Baptiste Alliette (1738–1791) writing under the pen name 'Etteilla'. It radically reordered the Major Arcana, placed a new card (Etteilla/The Questioner) as trump 1, and assigned detailed divinatory keywords — upright and reversed — to every card. Etteilla believed tarot had ancient Egyptian origins and created a comprehensive divinatory system more than a century before the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. The deck is sold today as 'Grand Etteilla' or 'Cartomancy Tarot'.
